title: Red teaming and safety evaluation
summary: Red teaming probes a system with adversarial inputs to find harms and security failures. Start with manual expert probing, then automate with PyRIT and the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent, score attack success rate, and review results by hand. Scans are non-deterministic and cover only the targets and categories each mode supports.
useIf: You are about to expose a model or agent to users, tools or untrusted content and must measure how it fails under attack.
avoidIf: You expect one scan to certify safety, or to run attacks against production systems that have real side effects.

explain.md: Microsoft's guidance is that red teaming is not a replacement for systematic measurement: complete an initial round of manual red teaming first to list the harms, then measure and mitigate. Mix experts with an adversarial mindset and ordinary users, assign testers to harms, and test the model, the application and both before and after mitigations [[tr2]].

The **AI Red Teaming Agent** uses Microsoft's open-source PyRIT [[r26]] together with Foundry risk and safety evaluations to scan, score and report. Its key metric is **attack success rate (ASR)**: successful attacks divided by total attacks. Limits: risk categories are text only, data is synthetic, mock tools only return data, and ASR is scored by a generative model, so it can be non-deterministic and produce false positives. Review before mitigating, and run in a purple environment (non-production with production-like resources) [[r5]]. Local mode is preview and not compatible with the new Foundry portal and SDK.

explain.title: Local scan (preview, azure-ai-evaluation[redteam], Python 3.10 to 3.13)
explain.code:
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.ai.evaluation.red_team import RedTeam, RiskCategory

red_team = RedTeam(
    azure_ai_project=project,                 # required
    credential=DefaultAzureCredential(),      # required
    risk_categories=[RiskCategory.Violence, RiskCategory.HateUnfairness],
    num_objectives=5,                         # default is 10
)
result = await red_team.scan(target=my_app_callback)
explain.caption: Targets can be a callback, an Azure OpenAI config or a PyRIT chat target [[r6]].
Where each mode applies (checked 2026-10-13)
head: Mode
Covers
Does not cover
rows: Text risk categories, single-turn only; complexity groups EASY (Base64, Flip, Morse), MODERATE (Tense), DIFFICULT (Tense with Base64). 4 categories x 1 objective x 4 strategies = 20 attack-response pairs [[r6]]
Prohibited actions, sensitive data leakage, task adherence, indirect prompt injection (XPIA). Targets: Foundry prompt agents and hosted container agents with Azure tool calls [[r5]]
Workflow agents, non-Foundry agents, function tool calls, browser automation, connected agents, computer use

explain.md: Regions differ between two Learn pages (five regions on the concept page, two on the limits page), so check both before promising a region [[r37]]. Public suites help too: HarmBench compares 18 red-teaming methods on 33 target models [[r43]], and AgentDojo has 97 tasks and 629 security test cases for prompt injection against tool-using agents [[r47]].

pitfalls.symptom: Attack success rate changes between identical scans
pitfalls.cause: ASR is scored by a generative model and attacks are sampled
pitfalls.fix: Review hits by hand, track trends across several scans and keep failing prompts as fixed regression cases

pitfalls.symptom: A scan reports zero risk for an agent with function tools
pitfalls.cause: Function tool calls are not supported by the cloud agentic scan
pitfalls.fix: Add manual tests and custom indirect-injection cases for those tools

pitfalls.symptom: Scan side effects appear in a real system
pitfalls.cause: The target was production with live tools
pitfalls.fix: Use a purple environment with production-like resources and mock or sandboxed tools

scenarios.title: Public text chatbot, no tools
scenarios.situation: A consumer chatbot answers general questions with no tools or retrieval. The harm concern is offensive and unsafe content. The team has a Foundry project and no red team.
scenarios.question: What do you run before launch?

options.name: A short manual round, then an automated scan across the four content categories and difficulty groups, with human review of hits
options.why: Manual probing lists the harms and the automated scan adds repeatable coverage. Review handles false positives.
options.tradeoff: Local mode is preview, and scans are single-turn and text only.

options.name: Rely on platform content filters only
options.why: Application-specific abuse and filter gaps stay unmeasured.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable as a baseline layer, never as the only evidence.

options.name: Run the public benchmark and ship
options.tradeoff: It does not reflect your prompt, users or mitigations.

flips.if: A retrieval source is added later

scenarios.takeaway: Manual first, automated for repeatability, humans review.

scenarios.title: Agent with function tools and customer data
scenarios.situation: A support agent calls function tools to read orders and send emails. Customer data and untrusted email text reach the model. The cloud agentic scan does not support function tool calls.
scenarios.question: How do you test for injection and data leakage?

options.name: Custom indirect-injection and leakage test cases against sandboxed tools, plus manual red team, with fixed regression cases
options.why: The automated agentic scan does not cover function tools, so you build the cases yourself and keep confirmed attacks as regressions.
options.tradeoff: Considerable authoring effort and no vendor ASR number.

options.name: Run the cloud agentic scan and report the result
options.why: Function tool calls are not supported, so the result would not cover the real risk.
options.tradeoff: It fits prompt agents or hosted agents using Azure tool calls.

options.name: Run the text-only local scan on the underlying model
options.tradeoff: It misses tool misuse and XPIA through your tools.

flips.if: Tools move to Azure tool calls on a Foundry agent

flips.then: Mock tool outputs and test the model decision only.

scenarios.takeaway: Know what the scan does not cover, then fill the gap.

scenarios.title: Weekly changes, regulated sector
scenarios.situation: An assistant in a regulated sector changes prompts and tools weekly. Compliance requires evidence for every release. A Foundry hosted agent uses Azure tool calls.
scenarios.question: How do you schedule red teaming?

options.name: Scheduled cloud scans each release, human triage, confirmed attacks added to a regression suite
options.why: Scheduling catches regressions from weekly change and triage controls false positives.
options.tradeoff: Preview features, regional limits and reviewer time.

options.name: One scan before launch
options.why: The system changes weekly, so the scan describes a past version.

flips.then: Add a full manual round each release.
Use local scans in a purple environment.

quiz.q: How is attack success rate (ASR) defined in the AI Red Teaming Agent?
options: Successful attacks divided by total attacks
Blocked attacks divided by total attacks
Attack strategies divided by risk categories
Findings reviewed by humans divided by findings
quiz.explain: ASR is successful attacks over total attacks. It is scored by a generative model, so it can be non-deterministic and needs review.

quiz.q: A local scan generates one attack objective for each of 4 risk categories and converts each baseline prompt with 4 attack strategies. The baseline prompts are sent too. How many attack-response pairs result?
quiz.explain: 4 baseline prompts + 4 x 4 converted prompts = 20, which matches the documented total of 20 attack-response pairs.

quiz.q: Which are documented limits of the AI Red Teaming Agent? Select all that apply.
options: ASR is scored by a generative model and may produce false positives
It can only attack models, never agents
Cloud agentic scans do not support function tool calls
quiz.explain: Judge noise, mock tools and unsupported function tools are documented limits. It also supports agents in the cloud, so option three is wrong.

flashcards.back: Attack success rate: successful attacks divided by total attacks. Scored by a generative model, so it can be non-deterministic and needs human review.

flashcards.front: Which targets does the cloud agentic red teaming support?
flashcards.back: Foundry prompt agents and hosted container agents with Azure tool calls. Not workflow agents, non-Foundry agents, function tool calls, browser automation, connected agents or computer use.
A non-production environment with production-like resources, used to run red team scans safely.
